title: Episode 142: The Impeachment of Andrew Johnson: The High Drama and the One-Vote Acquittal of 1868
description:
In May of 1868, the United States stood on the precipice of removing an elected president from office for the first time in its history. When Andrew Johnson defiantly fired Secretary of War Edwin Stanton in direct violation of the Tenure of Office Act, Congress struck with lightning speed. The House impeached Johnson on eleven articles of high crimes and misdemeanors, and the Senate transformed into a high court of justice presided over by Chief Justice Salmon P. Chase. This is the extraordinary story of the high-stakes legal combat, backroom political conspiracies, and the breathless Senate roll call where the presidency was saved by a single, agonizing vote.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our two-part investigation of Andrew Johnson by plunging directly into the heart of the most dramatic constitutional crisis of the nineteenth century: the first impeachment of an American president. With troops guarding Washington and the Secretary of War barricaded inside his office, the fate of the American executive branch hung upon the whispering lips of a freshman senator from Kansas. Here is George with the full story of the trial that shook the Republic.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE TRAP: THE TENURE OF OFFICE ACT
By early 1867, the enmity between Congress and President Andrew Johnson had curdled into utter paranoia. Congressional Republicans were convinced that Johnson intended to use his authority as Commander-in-Chief to dismantle military reconstruction in the South by removing loyal federal officers and replacing them with Southern sympathizers. The key bulwark standing between the President and the military was Secretary of War Edwin McMasters Stanton. Stanton, a fierce, iron-willed bureaucrat who had run Lincoln's war machine with ruthless efficiency, remained in Johnson's cabinet while secretly collaborating with Radical Republican leaders in Congress, funneling them confidential White House communications and advising them on legislative strategy.

To protect Stanton and rein in executive patronage, Congress passed the Tenure of Office Act on March 2, 1867, over Johnson's predictable veto. The statute boldly declared that any federal official appointed with the advice and consent of the Senate could not be removed by the President without the Senate's prior approval. To violate the act was declared a high misdemeanor, punishable by fine and imprisonment. Johnson and his legal advisors viewed the act as a flagrant, unconstitutional assault on the separation of powers. Even Lincoln's former attorney general, Edward Bates, privately believed the law crippled the executive. Johnson was determined to test the law in court, convinced that the Supreme Court would strike it down. In doing so, he stepped directly into the political bear trap Congress had laid at his feet.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SIEGE OF THE WAR DEPARTMENT
In August 1867, while Congress was out of session, Johnson suspended Stanton from office and appointed General Ulysses S. Grant as Secretary of War ad interim. Johnson believed Grant's enormous national popularity would insulate the administration from congressional retaliation. But when the Senate reconvened in January 1868 and formally voted to reinstate Stanton, Grant immediately locked the office doors, surrendered the keys, and stepped aside, refusing to defy federal law. Johnson was furious, accusing Grant of betrayal and cowardice during a tense White House cabinet meeting, an insult that permanently severed their friendship and pushed Grant into the arms of the Republican Party.

On February 21, 1868, Johnson made his fateful move. Defying the Senate's order, he officially fired Stanton and appointed Adjutant General Lorenzo Thomas, an aging, eccentric cavalry officer, as the new Secretary of War. Stanton refused to yield. When General Thomas arrived at the War Department to demand the keys, Stanton ordered him to leave. The two men engaged in an absurd shouting match before sharing a bottle of whiskey and parting company. But Stanton took no chances. He barricaded himself inside his second-floor office, posted armed guards at the doors, and slept on a military cot for weeks, eating takeout meals brought in by loyal clerks. The capital was gripped by rumors of military coups, civil war, and armed militias marching on the White House.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: HIGH CRIMES AND MISDEMEANORS
On Capitol Hill, the news of Stanton's removal hit like a bomb. Three days after Johnson issued his order, on February 24, 1868, the House of Representatives voted 126 to 47 along strict party lines to impeach Andrew Johnson, President of the United States, for high crimes and misdemeanors. A select committee drafted eleven articles of impeachment. Nine of the articles focused laser-like on the removal of Stanton and the violation of the Tenure of Office Act. The tenth article, penned by the bombastic Benjamin Butler of Massachusetts, accused Johnson of attempting to bring disgrace, ridicule, and contempt upon the Congress through his vulgar, abusive speeches during the Swing Around the Circle.

The eleventh article—crafted by the dying, frail, but relentlessly sharp-minded Thaddeus Stevens—was a masterwork of political indictment. It tied all of Johnson's actions together into a grand conspiracy: alleging that the President had systematically attempted to defeat the execution of the Reconstruction Acts, unlawfully control the military, and usurp the sovereign powers of the legislative branch. On March 5, Stevens, too weak to walk and carried into the Senate chamber in an armchair by two young Capitol pages, formally presented the articles of impeachment to the United States Senate. The great trial of the century had begun.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE COURT OF IMPEACHMENT AND CHIEF JUSTICE CHASE
Under the United States Constitution, the Chief Justice of the United States presides over the trial of an impeached president. Salmon P. Chase, an ambitious Ohio jurist who possessed his own White House dreams, ascended the dais of the Senate with formidable majesty. Radical Republicans had hoped Chase would act as an aggressive partisan partner in removing Johnson. Instead, Chase insisted on treating the Senate strictly as a judicial court of law, requiring formal rules of evidence, legal precedent, and solemn decorum. He repeatedly ruled that defense counsel must be permitted to present witnesses and make full legal arguments, infuriating House managers like Benjamin Butler, who wanted a swift political drumhead trial.

Johnson did not attend the proceedings, prudently remaining in the White House under the strict instructions of his brilliant legal defense team. That team was led by William M. Evarts of New York, one of the nation's most formidable appellate advocates, and former Supreme Court Justice Benjamin Robbins Curtis of Boston, who had written a famous, courageous dissent in the Dred Scott case. Curtis delivered a two-day opening argument of razor-sharp brilliance. He demonstrated that the Tenure of Office Act expressly protected cabinet members only 'during the term of the President by whom they were appointed.' Since Stanton had been appointed by Abraham Lincoln during Lincoln's first term in 1862, Stanton was not legally covered under the statute's protection during Johnson's administration. Furthermore, the defense argued, a president had the constitutional right to test the validity of an ambiguous federal law in court without being branded a criminal and removed from office.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE HIGH STAKES OF EDMUND ROSS
As the trial progressed into May, the math in the Senate became excruciatingly clear. There were fifty-four senators representing twenty-seven states. Under the Constitution, a two-thirds majority—thirty-six votes—was required to convict and remove the President. Twelve Democratic senators were certain to vote for acquittal. Six moderate Republican senators—William Pitt Fessenden of Maine, James Grimes of Iowa, John Henderson of Missouri, Lyman Trumbull of Illinois, Peter Van Winkle of West Virginia, and Joseph Fowler of Tennessee—had courageously broken ranks with their party, concluding that the charges did not rise to the level of high crimes and misdemeanors.

That left thirty-five solid votes for conviction. Exactly one more vote was needed to reach thirty-six and remove Johnson from the presidency. The entire fate of the republic rested upon a quiet, thirty-one-year-old freshman senator from Kansas named Edmund G. Ross. Ross was a former abolitionist newspaper editor and Union army major who had replaced the legendary James Lane following Lane's suicide. Radical leaders assumed Ross would toe the party line, but as the roll call approached, Ross remained stubbornly, maddeningly silent. Radical operatives placed him under 24-hour surveillance, rifled through his mail, and showered him with hundreds of threatening telegrams from Kansas constituents warning him that if he voted to acquit, he would suffer political death and social ostracism. Detectives followed him everywhere he went in Washington.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE ROLL CALL OF MAY 16, 1868
On Saturday, May 16, 1868, the Senate chamber was packed to suffocating capacity. Diplomatic envoys, cabinet secretaries, supreme court justices, and thousands of spectators crammed into the galleries, while a silent crowd spilled out onto the marble steps of the Capitol. Outside, the sky was dark and threatening. Radical leaders decided to vote first on the comprehensive Eleventh Article, believing it had the strongest chance of securing conviction. One by one, senators rose from their mahogany desks to answer 'Guilty' or 'Not Guilty.' The sick and dying were brought into the chamber to cast their ballots; Senator Grimes of Iowa, partially paralyzed by a stroke suffered two days earlier, was carried in by four men, his voice trembling as he whispered 'Not Guilty.'

When the clerk called the name of Mr. Ross, a suffocating silence fell over the chamber. Ross later recalled that looking down into the sea of furious, expectant faces felt like staring into an open grave. 'Mr. Senator Ross, how say you? Is the respondent, Andrew Johnson, guilty or not guilty of a high misdemeanor as charged in this article?' Ross stood, took a deep breath, and in a clear, firm voice that reached the back of the gallery, answered: 'Not Guilty.' A collective gasp tore through the gallery. The final tally was thirty-five Guilty, nineteen Not Guilty. The prosecution had failed by exactly one single vote. Ten days later, votes on the Second and Third Articles yielded the identical 35-to-19 result. Chief Justice Chase ordered the court adjourned sine die. Andrew Johnson had survived.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE CONSTITUTIONAL PRECEDENT AND THE LONG SHADOW
At the White House, when a telegraph boy arrived breathless with the news of Ross's vote, Andrew Johnson wept openly with relief. A bottle of whiskey was uncorked, and glasses were raised in celebration. Stanton immediately surrendered the keys to the War Department and vacated the building, his health permanently shattered. For the brave Republican senators who broke ranks, the political consequences were swift and brutal. Edmund Ross and all six of his fellow Republican dissenters were purged from the party, denied renomination, and hounded from public life by bitter constituents. Yet their sacrifice preserved a vital constitutional principle: that the presidency was an independent branch of government, and that a chief executive could not be deposed simply because an opposing legislative majority loathed his policies or his personality.

Johnson served out the remaining ten months of his presidency as a powerless figurehead, ignored by Congress and rejected by his own party for renomination in 1868. He returned home to Tennessee, but his thirst for vindication was unquenchable. In 1875, in an astonishing political comeback, the Tennessee state legislature elected Andrew Johnson back to the United States Senate. When the former president walked into the Senate chamber to take his oath, former adversaries who had voted to convict him seven years earlier watched in stunned silence as the gallery showered him with flowers. He died of a stroke just five months later, buried in Greeneville wrapped in an American flag with his head resting upon his worn, dog-eared copy of the United States Constitution.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The trial of Andrew Johnson established an enduring precedent that defined the American balance of powers for more than a century. While Johnson's obstructionism severely crippled the protection of newly freed slaves in the Reconstruction South, the failure to remove him ensured that the presidency would not devolve into a parliamentary office subservient to legislative whim. Next week, we turn to the man who succeeded him—the supreme Union hero of the Civil War, Ulysses S. Grant—and his historic rendezvous with Robert E. Lee at Appomattox. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
